title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 377
paragraphs: Hearing of this, Apries sent Amasis to them to put a stop to it by persuasion; and when he had come and was trying to restrain the Egyptians, as he was speaking and telling them not to revolt, one of the Egyptians stood up behind him and placed a helmet on his head, saying as he did so that he was putting it on to crown him king. To Amasis what was done was not entirely unwelcome, as he showed by his behavior; for as soon as the rebellious Egyptians had set him up as king, he prepared to march against Apries. Apries, hearing this, sent one of his own attendants to Amasis, a man of reputation whose name was Patarbemis, ordering him to bring Amasis alive into his presence. When Patarbemis came and summoned Amasis, the latter, who happened to be sitting on horseback, lifted up his leg and behaved in an unseemly manner, telling him to take that back to Apries. Nevertheless, they say, Patarbemis pressed him to go to the king, since the king had sent to summon him, and he replied that for some time past he had been preparing to do so, and that Apries would have no cause to fault him. Then Patarbemis, perceiving his intent both from what he said and from seeing his preparations, departed in haste, wishing to inform the king as quickly as possible of what was going on. When he returned to Apries without bringing Amasis, the king, paying no attention to what he said, but moved by violent anger, ordered his ears and nose to be cut off. And the rest of the Egyptians who still remained on his side, when they saw the man of greatest reputation among them suffering such shameful outrage, waited no longer but joined the others in revolt and delivered themselves over to Amasis.
